title: The golden lid
hook: the face of truth is hidden by a golden disc; uncover it (Isha Upanishad 15)
tomorrow: a monk crossing a desert kept saying one short text. which one?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salt in the water, salty from top to bottom, and two readings that land in one place. Hates no one.

Gold foil on a chocolate box. A glossy ad at one in the morning. A phone screen so bright you can't see past the shine to what's on it. The Isha Upanishad, near its end, names the thing hiding the truth, and it's gold. The face of truth is covered with a golden disc, it says. O Pushan, nourishing sun, uncover it, so that I, who love the truth, may see. The gold is the sun's own glare. The same lines also appear in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, as a prayer at the end of a life.
screen: `GOLD FOIL, GLOSSY ADS, GLARE.` → `THE FACE OF TRUTH...` → `...COVERED WITH A GOLDEN DISC.` → `UNCOVER IT.`

segments.voice: The Katha Upanishad tells a story about that lid. A boy named Nachiketa ends up at the door of Yama, the lord of death, and Yama grants him three wishes. For the third, Nachiketa asks: what happens after a person dies? Yama tries to talk him out of it. Ask for sons and grandsons who live a hundred years. Ask for cattle, horses, gold, a kingdom, a long life. Chariots, music, pleasures no one else could have. Nachiketa says: these last till tomorrow. Keep your horses, keep your dancing and songs. Tell me the thing I asked. Then Yama gives the teaching behind the test. There is the good, shreyas, and there is the pleasant, preyas. Both tie a person down. The wise choose the good; the foolish choose the pleasant. Set beside the Isha, that's one way to hear the golden lid. The pleasant isn't evil; it's gold. It just sits right on top of the truth, shining. And the Isha's verse doesn't ask to have the gold thrown away. It asks the sun itself to pull back its rays: uncover it. The next verse goes further: the light that is your fairest form, I see it. Behind the glare isn't darkness. It's more light.
screen: `NACHIKETA AT DEATH'S DOOR.` · `KEEP YOUR HORSES AND YOUR SONGS.` · `THE GOOD AND THE PLEASANT.` · then, large: `UNCOVER IT.`

segments.voice: Find one shiny thing near you: a ring, a coin, a spoon, a phone screen. Tilt it until it catches the light and let yourself enjoy the glint for a moment. Then hold it still and look past the shine to the thing itself, its shape, its weight, what it's actually for.
The golden lid: the Isha's picture of a bright covering over the face of truth, and the prayer to the sun to lift it.
Here's the line: uncover it, past the glint to the good. That's the Isha, all four days of it.

howItsDone: Hindus recite the Isha's closing verses, including 'the face of truth is covered with a golden disc', and they appear as a prayer for the dying in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad; the Katha's teaching of the good and the pleasant is studied alongside them.

fork.setup: two job offers: one flashy, with a big title and photos for your feed; one plainer, closer to what you care about. Yama's teaching, what's the question to ask?
options: which is the good, shreyas, and which is just the pleasant, preyas?
which one shines brighter? the Isha says gold is where truth shows.
neither: the Katha says turn down every good thing that's offered.
fork.reveal: Yama says both tie a person down, and the wise choose the good. the pleasant isn't evil; it just sits on top, shining.

original.note: Sanskrit, Isha Upanishad 15: by a golden vessel the face of truth is covered.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be shallow, look deeper.
what it means: the Isha asks the sun to draw back its bright disc so truth's face can be seen; read beside the Katha, the pleasant shines over the good the same way.
what a scholar hears: Isha 15–18 recur as a prayer of the dying in Brihadaranyaka 5.15; Katha 1.2.1–2 sets shreyas against preyas.

a crown worn by the lord of death in the Katha
the sun's disc, hiding nothing at all

chat.meaning: The pleasant shines over the good like a golden lid. Yama says the wise choose the good; the Isha asks the light to draw back.

Pushan.meaning: the nourishing sun god, asked to lift the golden disc

Nachiketa.meaning: the boy in the Katha Upanishad who questions death

Yama.meaning: the lord of death in Hindu tradition

shreyas.meaning: Sanskrit: the good, what truly helps

preyas.meaning: Sanskrit: the pleasant, what feels nice

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 15–16 (the face of truth covered by a golden disc; O Pushan, uncover it; the fairest form of your light I see)
Katha Upanishad 1.1.20–29 (Nachiketa's third wish; Yama's offers; 'these last till tomorrow; keep your horses, dance and song')
Katha Upanishad 1.2.1–2 (the good, shreyas, and the pleasant, preyas)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.15 (the same verses as a prayer at death)
